title: Kestrel live chat quickstart and recovery kickoff
summary: Introductory live demo of Redwood hosted API for chat/text generation. Focus on streaming behavior, key params (temperature, max_tokens), retry/backoff patterns, and recovery strategies. Customer asked about latency SLOs, SSO/KMS compliance, and fallbacks to lower-cost models.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-04 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Alicia Gomez (Kestrel CTO), Tom Rivers (Lead Frontend), Priya Nair (SRE)

[00:00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood, Maya is our SE, she'll do most of the demo. Quick agenda: 1) quick hosted API orientation 2) streaming behavior and params 3) retries and recovery patterns 4) console/Optimize touchpoints 5) Q&A and next steps. Sound good?

[00:00:12] Alicia Gomez: Yep that works for us. Thanks, Jordan. We're especially interested in how streaming behaves in our chat UI and what happens when the model hangs or we hit timeouts.

[00:00:25] Maya Patel: Awesome. I'll share my screen in a sec — just to set expectations, we're going to use the Redwood hosted chat endpoint, show streaming in a simple web client, tweak temperature and max_tokens, and then walk through retries and idempotency tokens. There will be a short console tour at the end for costs and tracing.

[00:00:42] Tom Rivers: Quick question before you start — our frontend is using long-poll style SSE. Will that map cleanly to the streaming API?

[00:00:50] Maya Patel: Yes, we expose streaming via server-sent events and websockets depending on the SDK. For plain REST you can use chunked transfer encoding or SSE. The payloads are incremental deltas — you get tokens as they generate. There are a couple of knobs we recommend on the client to make UX smooth: backpressure handling, a small buffer for partial tokens, and a timeout guard for partial responses.

[00:01:18] Priya Nair: And if a stream drops mid-response, what's our recommended recovery? Immediate retry? Resume?

[00:01:25] Maya Patel: Good question. There are two common patterns. First, idempotency + restart: attach an idempotency key to the request; if the stream times out, issue a retry that is recognized as the same conversation turn — Redwood server dedups duplicate tokens. Second, prefix caching or KV cache resume: if you're using short prefixes frequently, our runtime can cache KV state to resume from a known token index. For hosted customers we default to simple restart with backoff, and offer a resume API for larger sessions.

[00:01:58] Jordan Lee: One nuance to call out — for really low-latency use cases we advise tuning batch/window sizes and TTL of the KV cache. That trades off throughput (cost) vs latency.

[00:02:10] Alicia Gomez: What sort of latency numbers do people actually see in hosted mode? We want p95 under 300ms ideally for short replies (50-100 tokens).

[00:02:20] Maya Patel: For short replies with our optimized models and default region routing, median is often sub-150ms for token generation after request acceptance; p95 depends on payload size and concurrency, but sub-500ms for 50-token replies is typical. If you need strict 200-300ms p95 we recommend a dedicated pool or pinning to a model variant that trades accuracy for latency. Also consider our Optimize suggestions — it will recommend quantization + batching profiles to hit your cost/latency target.

[00:02:55] Tom Rivers: Okay. Demo please?

[00:03:00] Maya Patel: Sure — loading the sandbox console. (screen noise)

[00:03:12] [screen share sounds, typing]

[00:03:20] Maya Patel: Alright here's a simple web client we've wired to the Redwood hosted chat endpoint. I'll send a prompt: "Summarize the following patient note in one sentence: patient has mild cough, no fever, advised rest" and we'll stream.

[00:03:35] [00:03:35] Redwood Stream: {delta: "Patient with mild cough, afebrile, advised rest."}

[00:03:40] Tom Rivers: Nice, that's clean. How do you control tokenization? For example we need to ensure truncation doesn't break clinical terms.

[00:03:48] Maya Patel: We pass max_tokens and a stop sequence; also you can set logit_bias to discourage truncation mid-term for protected vocab, and configure tokenizer padding behavior. For clinical use we usually recommend an eval pass with your prompt set to find a sweet spot for max_tokens and stop.

[00:04:05] Alicia Gomez: Is there an automatic safety layer for PHI or do we need our own filters?

[00:04:12] Jordan Lee: Hosted API does not do PHI redaction by default. We provide hooks: you can run a pre-send filter using our console-integrated functions, or run post-response classification. For regulated customers we surface private deployment and provide on-prem options that keep data in your VPC; we also have KMS integrations.

[00:04:30] Priya Nair: Do you have SOC 2 and customer audit logs? We need to show auditors how keys are rotated and access is logged.

[00:04:38] Jordan Lee: Yes, we are SOC 2 Type II. We maintain detailed audit logs, SSO via SAML/OIDC, RBAC, and KMS integration for customer-managed keys. I'll attach the compliance pack after the call.

[00:04:54] Alicia Gomez: Thanks. Back to retries — what's the backoff strategy? Exponential? Jitter?

[00:05:01] Maya Patel: Exponential backoff with full jitter is our recommended default for client retries. For generation requests where you want to avoid duplicate content, use idempotency tokens and server-side deduping. We also expose a "retryable_error_codes" list in the SDK. For streaming we suggest a short initial wait (250-500ms) then exponential up to a couple of seconds for transient infra hiccups; for throttling errors we give you a Retry-After header.

[00:05:28] Tom Rivers: If we re-send the same turn and the model is non-deterministic, won't we get different text and confuse the conversation state?

[00:05:36] Maya Patel: That's why we support conversation-level caching and KV state snapshots — if you really need exactness you can snapshot the KV cache before generation and restore on retries. Another approach is to use deterministic seeds — set temperature to 0 and pin the model variant; that makes retries deterministic in most cases but changes creativity.

[00:05:56] Priya Nair: We're interested in cost — rough per-1k-token pricing? Ballpark is fine, we just need order of magnitude to plan a POC budget.

[00:06:04] Jordan Lee: I'll send the exact pricing in the sheet, but ballpark, hosted generation for an optimized open model is in the low single-digit cents per 1k tokens; higher for larger/fine-tuned variants. The big lever is batching and prefix cache hit rate — Optimize can suggest batching windows and quantization to reduce your unit cost by 20-40% depending on load.

[00:06:22] Alicia Gomez: Can Optimize run offline against our sample prompts to give a projection?

[00:06:27] Maya Patel: Yes, we can run a profiling job against your prompt set in our sandbox and give you a report with latency, cost estimates, and model recommendations. That'd be part of the POC.

[00:06:36] [00:06:36] Alejandro (sys): Uh sorry, wrong window — ignore that

[00:06:40] Tom Rivers: A few practical things: our frontend wants message-level acknowledgements in case of retries. How do you recommend we represent partial messages?

[00:06:48] Maya Patel: Use a message state machine: generating -> partial -> committed. On initial stream start, show partial content and attach the idempotency key; if a retry occurs, the client either merges the partial with resumed tokens or discards partials and replaces with committed final. We have a sample library that does this gracefully.

[00:07:10] Priya Nair: Any caveats about concurrency limits on hosted? We have bursty traffic and don't want throttles mid-day.

[00:07:16] Jordan Lee: Hosted tiers have soft concurrency limits by account to protect multi-tenant fairness. For bursty production traffic we recommend Redwood Dedicated or reserved capacity with autoscaling and burst pools. For onboarding POC hosted is usually fine, but we'll monitor metrics together.

[00:07:34] Alicia Gomez: Can the console show per-token cost breakdowns by route?

[00:07:38] Maya Patel: Yes — Console has per-route model breakdown, token counts, cost, and latency percentiles. You can drill into traces for slow requests and see the model variant and kernel selection. Optimize will also pop up suggestions (e.g., quantize this model to int8, reduce batch window, or fallback to smaller model on non-critical routes).

[00:07:58] Tom Rivers: You're mentioning kernel selection — is that visible to us or is it opaque?

[00:08:03] Maya Patel: Kernel selection is runtime-level telemetry. We surface higher-level signals in the console — model variant, quantization profile, and a compatibility note. Low-level kernel choices are currently internal, but we can share performance profile docs.

[00:08:18] Alicia Gomez: OK great. Let's do a failure simulation please — network drop during stream and a throttling case.

[00:08:25] Maya Patel: Cool — I'll simulate a dropped connection. Sending a long-form prompt now.

[00:08:35] [00:08:35] Redwood Stream: {delta: "The patient presents with..."}

[00:08:45] [network drop sound, typing]

[00:08:48] Maya Patel: And connection dropped. Client receives an EOF. In our sample client we immediately retry with the same idempotency key, wait 400ms then resume. Let's re-run —

[00:08:58] [00:08:58] Redwood Stream: {status: resumed, delta: "...chest pain but normal vitals. Recommended ECG and follow up."}

[00:09:05] Tom Rivers: Looks seamless. What if the retry goes to a different model variant?

[00:09:12] Maya Patel: If the routing policy changes (region or variant) you might see slightly different phrasing. For strict consistency we recommend pinning model versions in your rollout policy for critical paths. Alternatively, the fallback can be to an equivalent variant we guarantee parity for.

[00:09:28] Priya Nair: How do we set pinning? Is that via the console or API?

[00:09:33] Maya Patel: Both. In the Console you can create a route and pin a model config; via API pass a model_version parameter in the request. Canary rollouts are also supported — you can route X% of requests to a new variant and monitor quality regressions.

[00:09:48] Alicia Gomez: Any rough notes on security for hosted vs private? We may need HIPAA-level controls.

[00:09:55] Jordan Lee: For HIPAA workloads, many customers choose Redwood Private (VPC or on-prem) where the inference plane sits inside your network and we provide a control plane integration. We also offer customer-managed KMS keys and detailed audit logs. I'll include a HIPAA readiness note in the pack.

[00:10:12] Tom Rivers: One last thing — SDKs. Do you have idiomatic JS + Python libraries for streaming and automatic retries?

[00:10:19] Maya Patel: Yes — JS, Python, and a lightweight Go client. They handle SSE/websocket fallback, idempotency tokens, and have built-in retry strategies you can configure. We also have an example React component used in the demo.

[00:10:32] Alicia Gomez: Great. Back to next steps and timeline — we want a 2-week POC with a small sandbox and a profiling job. Can you support that timeline?

[00:10:40] Jordan Lee: Yes, that's reasonable. We'll provision a sandbox tenant and run a profiling job on your 200-sample prompts. Maya will coordinate the smoke test.

[00:10:48] Alicia Gomez: Perfect. Anything else from your side?

[00:10:52] Maya Patel: Just two small notes: 1) If you expect heavy concurrency, we can pre-warm a dedicated pool for the POC as an add-on; 2) For the profiling job we recommend including edge-case prompts that hit long-form and short-form extremes so we can give both latency and cost projections.

[00:11:10] Tom Rivers: Will do.

[00:11:15] Jordan Lee: Alright, let's recap. Action items: Jordan to send pricing + security docs; Maya to provision sandbox and run baseline profiling; Alicia to send prompt set and target SLOs. We'll set a 30-min POC benchmark slot next week. Anything to add?

[00:11:32] Alicia Gomez: No, that's all. Thanks, folks.

[00:11:36] Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email.

[00:11:40] [call ends]
